 Interim Relief Refused U/S 9 A&C Act Cannot Be Renewed In Suit Against Same Parties: Madras High Court Declines To Restrain OTT Release Of Drishyam 3
 The Court also held that the plaintiff had not prima facie shown a subsisting right to prevent the original producer and director from assigning adaptation rights.
 By Agatha Shukla Loading... | 17 Nov 2026 1:00 PM IST X The Madras High Court has held that a plaintiff whose application under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 for an interim injunction was dismissed on merits cannot seek the very same relief, against the same respondents and on the same documents, by filing a suit. On this footing, the Court refused to restrain the OTT release of the Hindi film “Dhrishyam 3: The Conclusion”.
 The Court also held that the plaintiff, Rajkumar Theatres Pvt Ltd, had not prima facie shown a subsisting right to prevent the producer and director of the Malayalam film “Dhrishyam” from assigning its adaptation rights. It dismissed the original application in the commercial suit without costs.
 Earlier, on October 1, 2026, another Single Judge Bench had dismissed the plaintiff’s application under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 seeking to restrain the worldwide release and exploitation of the Hindi film, holding that the plaintiff had not made out a case for an interim injunction. The plaintiff did not appeal and instead filed the present suit, renewing the same relief against the same respondents, now limited to the OTT release.
 A Single Bench of Justice P.B. Balaji observed, “…having suffered a dismissal in the Section 9 application, where the very same relief has been sought for, against the very same respondents as well, and the said order dated 01.10.2026 having become final, the applicant/plaintiff cannot and is not entitled to an interim injunction, merely because the applicant/plaintiff has chosen to abandon the arbitration route and has instead filed the present suit wherein the very same interim relief has been renewed. Though there may be change in circumstances, as held in Vishnu Traders case as well as in K.K. Modi case (referred in supra), the interlocutory orders also have to be respected, unless exceptional facts and circumstances are made out as to any change in factual position, entitling the applicant/plaintiff to interim relief in the 2nd action despite having suffered an adverse order in an earlier action”. 
 Senior Advocate K. Ravi appeared for the plaintiff, while Senior Advocate Sathish Parasaran appeared for respondents 2 and 3, Senior Advocate P.S. Raman appeared for respondent 4, and Advocate K. Manoj Menon for respondent 5.
 “Dhrishyam” was produced by respondent 2 and directed by respondent 3, and was released in 2013. In 2013, they granted respondent 1 exclusive rights to remake, dub and adapt it, including its sequels, in Hindi and other North Indian languages. In 2014, respondent 1 and the plaintiff agreed to jointly develop the Hindi remake and share profits equally. In 2024, they assigned Hindi remake rights to Viacom 18, whose rights now lie with respondent 4. On November 22, 2025, respondents 2 and 3 assigned adaptation rights of the script in Hindi to respondent 5 for Rs. 15 crore.
 The plaintiff first filed a Section 9 application against all the respondents just before the film’s release. It was dismissed on merits on October 1, 2026, and no appeal was filed. The film was released in theatres on October 2, 2026. The plaintiff then filed a suit and this application, which pressed only the OTT release. The suit and application were given up against respondents 6 and 7, and respondent 1 filed no counter.
 Reading the four agreements together, the Court held that the plaintiff received only the Hindi remake right in the original film, a commercial arrangement and not an assignment of copyright. It noted the plaintiff had not pleaded, even after the release, that the film was a sequel of “Dhrishyam 2”, and that the censor certificate carries the title “The Conclusion”. It held that the plaintiff, not being a party to the agreement, could not challenge the Rs. 15 crore payment as collusive.
 On res judicata, the Court held that the Section 9 order was on merits, that the parties, cause of action and documents were the same, and that the plaintiff, having impleaded respondents 2 to 7 voluntarily, should have appealed. 
 The Court clarified that this does not stretch to denying the plaintiff relief in the main suit.
 Cause Title: Rajkumar Theatres Pvt Ltd v. Wide Angle Creations & 6 Ors., OA No. 1114 of 2026 in C.S. (Comm Div) No. 280 of 2026 
 Appearances: 
 Applicant : K. Ravi, Sr. Counsel, R. Murugan.
 Respondents : P.S. Raman, Sr. Counsel, Rahul Balaji (R4); Sathish Parasaran, Sr. Counsel, Akshaya Ramadurai (R2 and R3); K. Manoj Menon (R5); Sowjanya Shyam, Sharath Chandran (R1).
